title: Module Documentation, Imports, and Namespace
content:
The module docstring introduces the general truncation divisibility rule as an answer to the open question from `divisibility-by-3-oq-01`: can all truncation rules be unified into a single parametric theorem?

The answer is YES, via two general theorems (positive and negative osculators) that subsume ALL specific truncation rules for divisors coprime to 10. The key algebraic identity $10 \cdot (n/10 + c \cdot (n\%10)) = n + (10c - 1) \cdot (n\%10)$ drives both theorems.

Imports only `Mathlib.Data.Nat.Digits.Defs` (for digit-related lemmas) and `Mathlib.Tactic` (for `linear_combination`, `push_cast`, `omega`, `norm_num`, `decide`). Opens `Nat` for natural number notation.
mathContext: The osculator method: for $d$ coprime to 10, the multiplicative inverse $c = 10^{-1} \bmod d$ gives $d \mid n \iff d \mid (\lfloor n/10 \rfloor + c \cdot (n \bmod 10))$. The negative osculator uses $c = -(10^{-1}) \bmod d$.

title: Division-Modulus Identity in Z
content:
The foundation: $n = 10 \cdot \lfloor n/10 \rfloor + (n \bmod 10)$ cast to $\mathbb{Z}$, proved by `push_cast; omega` using `Nat.div_add_mod`. This is used as `hdiv` in both main theorems via `linear_combination -hdiv`.

The `push_cast` tactic lifts the natural number identity to integers, and `omega` handles the resulting linear arithmetic. This two-tactic proof is remarkably clean — the identity is the algebraic engine for the entire development.
mathContext:
In $\mathbb{Z}$: $n = 10 \cdot \lfloor n/10 \rfloor + (n \bmod 10)$, lifted from `Nat.div_add_mod` via `push_cast`.

This is the pivotal identity that `linear_combination -hdiv` exploits: negating it gives $0 = -n + 10q + r$ where $q = n/10$ and $r = n\%10$.

title: General Positive Osculator Theorem
content:
The main theorem `truncation_pos`: for any $d$ coprime to 10 and $c$ satisfying $d \mid (10c-1)$, we have $d \mid n \iff d \mid (\lfloor n/10 \rfloor + c \cdot (n\%10))$.

The proof constructs the key intermediate expression $10 \cdot (q + c \cdot r)$ where $q = n/10$ and $r = n\%10$. The algebraic identity $10(q + cr) = n + (10c-1)r$ is proved by `linear_combination -hdiv`. Since $d \mid (10c-1)$, the correction term $(10c-1)r$ is divisible by $d$, so $d \mid n \iff d \mid 10(q+cr)$. Finally, $\gcd(d,10) = 1$ (from `IsCoprime`) allows canceling the factor 10 via `IsCoprime.dvd_of_dvd_mul_left`.

Examples: $d = 13$, $c = 4$ (since $39 = 3 \times 13$); $d = 19$, $c = 2$ (since $19 = 19$).
mathContext:
$10(\lfloor n/10 \rfloor + c(n \bmod 10)) = n + (10c-1)(n \bmod 10)$

When $d \mid (10c-1)$ and $\gcd(d,10) = 1$:
$d \mid n \iff d \mid n + (10c-1)(n\%10) = 10(q + cr) \iff d \mid (q + cr)$

title: General Negative Osculator Theorem
content:
Symmetric theorem `truncation_neg` for the negative osculator: $d \mid (10c+1)$ gives $d \mid n \iff d \mid (\lfloor n/10 \rfloor - c \cdot (n\%10))$.

The identity is $10(q - cr) = n - (10c+1)r$. When $d \mid (10c+1)$, we have $10c \equiv -1 \pmod{d}$, meaning $c$ is the 'negative inverse' of 10 mod $d$.

Canonical examples: $d = 7$, $c = 2$ (since $21 = 3 \times 7$); $d = 11$, $c = 1$ (since $11 = 11$); $d = 17$, $c = 5$ (since $51 = 3 \times 17$). The $d = 11$ case with $c = 1$ reduces to the alternating digit-sum rule: subtracting the last digit from the truncated number is equivalent to the classical alternating sum test.
mathContext:
$10(\lfloor n/10 \rfloor - c(n \bmod 10)) = n - (10c+1)(n \bmod 10)$

When $d \mid (10c+1)$ and $\gcd(d,10) = 1$:
$d \mid n \iff d \mid (q - cr)$

The negative osculator $c$ satisfies $10c \equiv -1 \pmod{d}$, i.e., $c \equiv -10^{-1} \pmod{d}$.

title: 11 Concrete Corollaries: Classical Rules Recovered
content:
Each classical divisibility rule is recovered as a one-line corollary of the general theorems. The proofs are: instantiate the general theorem with specific $d$ and $c$, verify coprimality by `decide`, and verify the osculator equation by `⟨k, by norm_num⟩`.

The osculator table:
| $d$ | Type | $c$ | Equation | Factor |
|-----|------|-----|----------|--------|
| 3 | pos | 1 | $9 = 3 \times 3$ | digit sum |
| 7 | neg | 2 | $21 = 3 \times 7$ | classical |
| 9 | pos | 1 | $9 = 1 \times 9$ | digit sum |
| 11 | neg | 1 | $11 = 1 \times 11$ | alternating sum |
| 13 | pos | 4 | $39 = 3 \times 13$ | classical |
| 17 | neg | 5 | $51 = 3 \times 17$ | classical |
| 19 | pos | 2 | $19 = 1 \times 19$ | classical |
| 23 | pos | 7 | $69 = 3 \times 23$ | classical |
| 29 | pos | 3 | $29 = 1 \times 29$ | classical |
| 31 | neg | 3 | $31 = 1 \times 31$ | classical |
| 37 | neg | 11 | $111 = 3 \times 37$ | classical |
mathContext: Each corollary is proved by: `truncation_pos d c n (by decide) ⟨k, by norm_num⟩` or `truncation_neg d c n (by decide) ⟨k, by norm_num⟩`. The `decide` verifies $\gcd(d,10) = 1$ and `norm_num` verifies $10c \mp 1 = k \cdot d$.

title: Osculator Table Verification and Sanity Checks
content:
Two sets of `example` declarations verify the framework:

1. **Osculator table**: Each positive osculator satisfies $d \mid (10c - 1)$ and each negative osculator satisfies $d \mid (10c + 1)$, verified by explicit witnesses.

2. **Sanity checks**: Specific numeric examples demonstrate the rules in action:
- $7 \mid 49$: $49 \to 4 - 2 \cdot 9 = -14$, and $7 \mid -14$ \checkmark
- $13 \mid 169$: $169 \to 16 + 4 \cdot 9 = 52$, and $13 \mid 52$ \checkmark
- $19 \mid 57$: $57 \to 5 + 2 \cdot 7 = 19$, and $19 \mid 19$ \checkmark
- $17 \mid 51$: $51 \to 5 - 5 \cdot 1 = 0$, and $17 \mid 0$ \checkmark

These use `native_decide` for the natural number divisibility and explicit witnesses for the truncated form.
mathContext: The sanity checks verify the truncation steps manually: $n \to \lfloor n/10 \rfloor \pm c \cdot (n \bmod 10)$. Each step reduces a multi-digit number to a smaller one while preserving divisibility.

title: Summary Theorem: Five Classical Cases Unified
content:
The master theorem `truncation_method_summary` packages the positive and negative osculator results for $d \in \{3, 7, 9, 11, 13\}$ into a single conjunction, demonstrating that all five classical divisibility rules are one-line consequences of the general framework.

This unifies: digit-sum rules ($d = 3, 9$ via positive osculator $c = 1$), alternating digit-sum ($d = 11$ via negative osculator $c = 1$), and classical truncation rules ($d = 7$ neg, $d = 13$ pos) under a single algebraic principle.

The proof is a conjunction of the five specific corollaries, each itself a one-liner from the general theorems. This demonstrates the power of the parametric approach: dozens of seemingly ad-hoc pencil-and-paper tricks reduce to instances of two theorems.
mathContext:
Unified theorem: $\bigwedge_{d \in \{3,7,9,11,13\}} (d \mid n \iff d \mid f_d(\lfloor n/10 \rfloor, n \bmod 10))$

where $f_d$ is either $q + c_d r$ (positive) or $q - c_d r$ (negative) depending on $d$.
